text: This course is for people whose daily work is SQL, dbt, and notebooks — not a generic software-engineering audience. Every example grounds itself in a real data project.

Every Git operation moves a change through three stages: the working directory, where you're actually editing files; the staging area, where you deliberately choose what goes into the next commit; and the repository, the permanent saved history. That staging step is what surprises people coming from a "just save the file" workflow — Git never assumes you want to save everything you've touched.

Without version control: filename-based versioning like "final_v2_ACTUALLY_final.sql." A dashboard breaks and nobody can say what changed in the query behind it. Two analysts edit the same dbt model the same afternoon, and one silently overwrites the other. Git solves all of this directly — every change becomes a timestamped, attributed, permanent snapshot.
Next lesson: installing Git and creating your first real repository.
